translations.title: What are Scaled Copies?
translations.explanation: What are Scaled Copies? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Scale Drawings”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.G.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, including computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing a scale drawing at a different scale. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: What are Scaled Copies?. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 4 and 2 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 4 × 2 = 8 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 7 and 5 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 7 × 5 = 35 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 4 and 2. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 8. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 7 and 5. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 35. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: What are Scaled Copies?. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: What are Scaled Copies?. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Geometria — What are Scaled Copies?
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Geometria — What are Scaled Copies?” należy do działu „Scale Drawings” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:7.G.A.1. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń opisuje, składa, rozkłada, porównuje i analizuje figury na podstawie ich cech definiujących, a nie wyłącznie wyglądu. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Geometria — What are Scaled Copies?. Wnioski geometryczne powinny opierać się na takich własnościach jak boki, kąty, proste równoległe lub prostopadłe, symetria, współrzędne, przystawanie, podobieństwo albo równe części. Rysunek jest dowodem tylko wtedy, gdy znane lub zaznaczone własności uzasadniają wniosek.

Krok 4: zauważ, że obrót figury nie zmienia jej własności. Krok 1: rozpoznaj cechy definiujące: cztery boki i cztery kąty proste. Krok 2: użyj długości 7 i 5. Krok 3: pomnóż i otrzymaj pole 35. translations.title: Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables
translations.explanation: Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Introducing Proportional Relationships”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.RP.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities. a. Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin. b. Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships. c. Represent proportional relationships by equations. For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn. d. Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate. Instructional focus: Students compare quantities multiplicatively and use equivalent ratios, unit rates, tables, graphs, equations, and percentages to describe proportional relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables. A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios scale both quantities by the same nonzero factor. In y = kx, k is the constant of proportionality and equals the unit rate when the variables have the corresponding units.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The ratio 6:5 is equivalent to 12:10 because both terms were multiplied by 2. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 5/6 = 0.833. Example 2: The ratio 4:6 is equivalent to 16:24 because both terms were multiplied by 4. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 6/4 = 1.5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: preserve the order 6:5. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 2. Step 3: obtain 12:10. Step 4: divide 5 by 6 to obtain unit rate 0.833 and retain the contextual units. Step 1: preserve the order 4:6. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 4. Step 3: obtain 16:24. Step 4: divide 6 by 4 to obtain unit rate 1.5 and retain the contextual units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables. Do not compare ratios using only one component. Keep units and order consistent. A relationship with a nonzero intercept is not directly proportional, even if some pairs look almost proportional.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables. State the ratio with units and order, find an equivalent ratio or unit rate, represent the relationship, and check that both quantities scale consistently.

translations.title: Stosunki i proporcjonalność — Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Stosunki i proporcjonalność — Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables” należy do działu „Introducing Proportional Relationships” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:7.RP.A.2. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń porównuje wielkości w sposób multiplikatywny i wykorzystuje równoważne stosunki, stawki jednostkowe, tabele, wykresy, równania oraz procenty do opisu proporcjonalności. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki i proporcjonalność — Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables. Stosunek porównuje dwie wielkości w ustalonej kolejności. Stosunki równoważne powstają przez pomnożenie obu wielkości przez ten sam niezerowy czynnik. W równaniu y = kx liczba k jest stałą proporcjonalności i odpowiada stawce jednostkowej.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Stosunek 6:5 jest równoważny 12:10, ponieważ obie liczby pomnożono przez 2. Druga wielkość na jedną jednostkę pierwszej wynosi 5/6 = 0.833. Przykład 2: Stosunek 4:6 jest równoważny 16:24, ponieważ obie liczby pomnożono przez 4. Druga wielkość na jedną jednostkę pierwszej wynosi 6/4 = 1.5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 6:5. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 2. Krok 3: otrzymaj 12:10. Krok 4: podziel 5 przez 6, aby otrzymać stawkę jednostkową 0.833, i zachowaj jednostki z kontekstu. Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 4:6. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 4. Krok 3: otrzymaj 16:24. Krok 4: podziel 6 przez 4, aby otrzymać stawkę jednostkową 1.5, i zachowaj jednostki z kontekstu.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki i proporcjonalność — Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables. Nie porównuj stosunków na podstawie tylko jednej liczby. Zachowuj kolejność i jednostki. Zależność z niezerowym wyrazem wolnym nie jest proporcjonalnością prostą, nawet jeśli część punktów wygląda podobnie.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki i proporcjonalność — Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables. Zapisz stosunek z jednostkami i właściwą kolejnością, wyznacz równoważny stosunek lub stawkę jednostkową, przedstaw zależność i sprawdź zgodne skalowanie obu wielkości.

translations.title: Exploring Circles
translations.explanation: Exploring Circles is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Measuring Circles”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.G.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Draw (freehand, with ruler and protractor, and with technology) geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Exploring Circles. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 5 and 7 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 5 × 7 = 35 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 9 and 2 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 9 × 2 = 18 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 5 and 7. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 35. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 9 and 2. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 18. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Exploring Circles. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Exploring Circles. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Circumference and Wheels
translations.explanation: Circumference and Wheels is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Measuring Circles”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.G.B.4, CCSS:7.RP.A.2, CCSS:7.RP.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle. Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities. a. Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin. b. Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships. c. Represent proportional relationships by equations. For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn. d. Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Circumference and Wheels. A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Applying Area of Circles. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 7 and 2 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 7 × 2 = 14 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 9 and 4 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 9 × 4 = 36 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 7 and 2. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 14. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 9 and 4. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 36. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Applying Area of Circles. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Applying Area of Circles. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Applying Pole of Okręgi

For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. translations.title: Ratios and Rates With Fractions
translations.explanation: Ratios and Rates With Fractions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Proportional Relationships and Percentages”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.RP.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units. For example, if a person walks 1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour, c ompute the unit rate as the complex fraction 1/2/1/4 miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour. Instructional focus: Students compare quantities multiplicatively and use equivalent ratios, unit rates, tables, graphs, equations, and percentages to describe proportional relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Ratios and Rates With Fractions. A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios scale both quantities by the same nonzero factor. In y = kx, k is the constant of proportionality and equals the unit rate when the variables have the corresponding units.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The ratio 7:3 is equivalent to 14:6 because both terms were multiplied by 2. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 3/7 = 0.429. Example 2: The ratio 8:5 is equivalent to 32:20 because both terms were multiplied by 4. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 5/8 = 0.625.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: preserve the order 7:3. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 2. Step 3: obtain 14:6. Step 4: divide 3 by 7 to obtain unit rate 0.429 and retain the contextual units. Step 1: preserve the order 8:5. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 4. Step 3: obtain 32:20. Step 4: divide 5 by 8 to obtain unit rate 0.625 and retain the contextual units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Ratios and Rates With Fractions. Do not compare ratios using only one component. Keep units and order consistent. A relationship with a nonzero intercept is not directly proportional, even if some pairs look almost proportional.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Ratios and Rates With Fractions. State the ratio with units and order, find an equivalent ratio or unit rate, represent the relationship, and check that both quantities scale consistently.

translations.title: Stosunki and Rates With Ułamki
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Stosunki and Rates With Ułamki” należy do działu „Proportional Relationships and Percentages” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:7.RP.A.1. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń porównuje wielkości w sposób multiplikatywny i wykorzystuje równoważne stosunki, stawki jednostkowe, tabele, wykresy, równania oraz procenty do opisu proporcjonalności. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki and Rates With Ułamki. Stosunek porównuje dwie wielkości w ustalonej kolejności. Stosunki równoważne powstają przez pomnożenie obu wielkości przez ten sam niezerowy czynnik. W równaniu y = kx liczba k jest stałą proporcjonalności i odpowiada stawce jednostkowej.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Stosunek 7:3 jest równoważny 14:6, ponieważ obie liczby pomnożono przez 2. Druga wielkość na jedną jednostkę pierwszej wynosi 3/7 = 0.429. Przykład 2: Stosunek 8:5 jest równoważny 32:20, ponieważ obie liczby pomnożono przez 4. Druga wielkość na jedną jednostkę pierwszej wynosi 5/8 = 0.625.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 7:3. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 2. Krok 3: otrzymaj 14:6. Krok 4: podziel 3 przez 7, aby otrzymać stawkę jednostkową 0.429, i zachowaj jednostki z kontekstu. Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 8:5. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 4. Krok 3: otrzymaj 32:20. Krok 4: podziel 5 przez 8, aby otrzymać stawkę jednostkową 0.625, i zachowaj jednostki z kontekstu.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki and Rates With Ułamki. Nie porównuj stosunków na podstawie tylko jednej liczby. Zachowuj kolejność i jednostki. Zależność z niezerowym wyrazem wolnym nie jest proporcjonalnością prostą, nawet jeśli część punktów wygląda podobnie.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki and Rates With Ułamki. Zapisz stosunek z jednostkami i właściwą kolejnością, wyznacz równoważny stosunek lub stawkę jednostkową, przedstaw zależność i sprawdź zgodne skalowanie obu wielkości.

translations.title: Revisiting Proportional Relationships
translations.explanation: Revisiting Proportional Relationships is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Proportional Relationships and Percentages”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.RP.A.1, CCSS:7.RP.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units. For example, if a person walks 1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour, c ompute the unit rate as the complex fraction 1/2/1/4 miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour. Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities. a. Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin. b. Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships. c. Represent proportional relationships by equations. For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn. d. Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate. Instructional focus: Students compare quantities multiplicatively and use equivalent ratios, unit rates, tables, graphs, equations, and percentages to describe proportional relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

Interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts. b. Understand that integers can be divided, provided that the divisor is not zero, and every quotient of integers (with non-zero divisor) is a rational number. If p and q are integers, then –(p/q) = (–p)/q = p/(–q). Interpret quotients of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts. Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships. c. Represent proportional relationships by equations. For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relation... The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Start at -9 on the number line and add 4. Moving 4 units to the right lands at -5, so -9 + 4 = -5. The absolute value |-9| = 9. translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: locate -9. Step 2: addition of positive 4 means move right 4 units. Step 3: arrive at -5. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-9|=9 records distance from zero, not the sign. Step 1: locate -8. Step 2: addition of positive 8 means move right 8 units. Step 3: arrive at 0. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-8|=8 records distance from zero, not the sign.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Say It with Decimals. Do not confuse a negative sign with an instruction to subtract. When comparing negative numbers, the number farther left is smaller. Keep exact values, such as radicals, when a decimal approximation is not required.

translations.title: Interpreting Negative Numbers
translations.explanation: Interpreting Negative Numbers is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Rational Number Arithmetic”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.NS.A.1, CCSS:7.NS.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram. a. Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0. For example, a hydrogen atom has 0 charge because its two constituents are oppositely charged. b. Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts. c. Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p – q = p + (–q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts. d. Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers. Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division and of fractions to multiply and divide rational numbers. a. Understand that multiplication is extended from fractions to rational numbers by requiring that operations continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as (–1)(–1) = 1 and the rules for multiply... Instructional focus: Students extend arithmetic to signed, rational, and irrational numbers and reason about magnitude, order, opposites, absolute value, and operations on the number line. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Interpreting Negative Numbers. Position on the number line determines order. Opposites are the same distance from zero on different sides. Absolute value is distance from zero. Operation rules must be connected to direction, magnitude, or properties rather than memorized without meaning.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Start at -12 on the number line and add 6. Moving 6 units to the right lands at -6, so -12 + 6 = -6. The absolute value |-12| = 12. Example 2: Start at -9 on the number line and add 5. Moving 5 units to the right lands at -4, so -9 + 5 = -4. The absolute value |-9| = 9.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: locate -12. Step 2: addition of positive 6 means move right 6 units. Step 3: arrive at -6. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-12|=12 records distance from zero, not the sign. Step 1: locate -9. Step 2: addition of positive 5 means move right 5 units. Step 3: arrive at -4. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-9|=9 records distance from zero, not the sign.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Interpreting Negative Numbers. Do not confuse a negative sign with an instruction to subtract. When comparing negative numbers, the number farther left is smaller. Keep exact values, such as radicals, when a decimal approximation is not required.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Interpreting Negative Numbers. Represent the numbers on an appropriate scale, apply operation and order rules carefully, and check sign and magnitude before accepting the result.

translations.title: Interpreting Negative Liczby

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń rozszerza działania na liczby ze znakiem, wymierne i niewymierne oraz analizuje ich wielkość, porządek, liczby przeciwne, wartość bezwzględną i działania na osi liczbowej. Liczby przeciwne leżą w tej samej odległości od zera po przeciwnych stronach. Wartość bezwzględna oznacza odległość od zera. Reguły działań warto wiązać z kierunkiem, wielkością i własnościami.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Zacznij w punkcie -12 na osi liczbowej i dodaj 6. Przesunięcie o 6 w prawo prowadzi do -6, więc -12 + 6 = -6. Wartość bezwzględna |-12| = 12. Przykład 2: Zacznij w punkcie -9 na osi liczbowej i dodaj 5. Przesunięcie o 5 w prawo prowadzi do -4, więc -9 + 5 = -4. Wartość bezwzględna |-9| = 9.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zaznacz -12. Krok 2: dodanie dodatniej liczby 6 oznacza ruch o 6 w prawo. Krok 3: otrzymujesz -6. Krok 4: sprawdź znak i wielkość; |-12|=12 oznacza odległość od zera. Krok 1: zaznacz -9. Krok 2: dodanie dodatniej liczby 5 oznacza ruch o 5 w prawo. Krok 3: otrzymujesz -4. Krok 4: sprawdź znak i wielkość; |-9|=9 oznacza odległość od zera.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Interpreting Negative Liczby. Nie myl znaku liczby ujemnej z działaniem odejmowania. Przy porównywaniu liczb ujemnych liczba położona bardziej w lewo jest mniejsza. Zachowuj wartości dokładne, np. pierwiastki, jeśli przybliżenie dziesiętne nie jest potrzebne.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Interpreting Negative Liczby. Przedstaw liczby na odpowiedniej skali, ostrożnie zastosuj reguły działań i porządku oraz sprawdź znak i wielkość wyniku.

translations.title: Negative Rates
translations.explanation: Negative Rates is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Rational Number Arithmetic”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.EE.B.3, CCSS:7.NS.A.3, CCSS:7.RP.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies. For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation. Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.1 1Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions. Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities. a. Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin. b. Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional... Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Negative Rates. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 4x + 3 = 27. Subtract 3 and divide by 4; the solution is x = 6. Example 2: Solve 5x + 4 = 29. Subtract 4 and divide by 5; the solution is x = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 3 from both sides to get 4x = 24. Step 2: divide both sides by 4. Step 3: x=6. Step 4: substitute: 4(6)+3=27, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 4 from both sides to get 5x = 25. Step 2: divide both sides by 5. Step 3: x=5. Step 4: substitute: 5(5)+4=29, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Negative Rates. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Negative Rates. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

translations.title: Solving Problems with Rational Numbers
translations.explanation: Solving Problems with Rational Numbers is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Rational Number Arithmetic”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.NS.A.3, CCSS:7.RP.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.1 1Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions. Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities. a. Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin. b. Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships. c. Represent proportional relationships by equations. For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn. d. Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate. Instructional focus: Students extend arithmetic to signed, rational, and irrational numbers and reason about magnitude, order, opposites, absolute value, and operations on the number line. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Problems with Rational Numbers. Position on the number line determines order. Opposites are the same distance from zero on different sides. Absolute value is distance from zero. Operation rules must be connected to direction, magnitude, or properties rather than memorized without meaning.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Start at -12 on the number line and add 5. Moving 5 units to the right lands at -7, so -12 + 5 = -7. The absolute value |-12| = 12. Example 2: Start at -7 on the number line and add 8. Moving 8 units to the right lands at 1, so -7 + 8 = 1. The absolute value |-7| = 7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: locate -12. Step 2: addition of positive 5 means move right 5 units. Step 3: arrive at -7. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-12|=12 records distance from zero, not the sign. Step 1: locate -7. Step 2: addition of positive 8 means move right 8 units. Step 3: arrive at 1. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-7|=7 records distance from zero, not the sign.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Problems with Rational Numbers. Do not confuse a negative sign with an instruction to subtract. When comparing negative numbers, the number farther left is smaller. Keep exact values, such as radicals, when a decimal approximation is not required.

translations.title: Solving Equations with Rational Numbers
translations.explanation: Solving Equations with Rational Numbers is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Rational Number Arithmetic”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.EE.B.4, CCSS:7.NS.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities. a. Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach. For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width? b. Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions. Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.1 1Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Equations with Rational Numbers. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 4x + 7 = 31. Subtract 7 and divide by 4; the solution is x = 6. Example 2: Solve 6x + 4 = 34. Subtract 4 and divide by 6; the solution is x = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 7 from both sides to get 4x = 24. Step 2: divide both sides by 4. Step 3: x=6. Step 4: substitute: 4(6)+7=31, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 4 from both sides to get 6x = 30. Step 2: divide both sides by 6. Step 3: x=5. Step 4: substitute: 6(5)+4=34, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Equations with Rational Numbers. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Solving Equations with Rational Numbers. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń wykorzystuje własności działań i działania odwrotne do zapisywania, interpretowania, przekształcania i rozwiązywania wyrażeń, równań oraz nierówności. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Reasoning about Solving Równania (Part 1). Wyrażenie opisuje wartość, równanie stwierdza równość dwóch wyrażeń, a nierówność je porównuje. Przekształcenia równoważne zachowują zbiór rozwiązań. Podstawienie pozwala sprawdzić, czy dana wartość spełnia relację.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Rozwiąż 3x + 1 = 7. Odejmij 1 i podziel przez 3; otrzymujemy x = 2. Przykład 2: Rozwiąż 4x + 4 = 40. Odejmij 4 i podziel przez 4; otrzymujemy x = 9.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: odejmij 1 od obu stron: 3x = 6. Krok 2: podziel obie strony przez 3. Krok 3: x=2. Krok 4: sprawdzenie: 3(2)+1=7, więc równanie jest spełnione. Krok 1: odejmij 4 od obu stron: 4x = 36. Krok 2: podziel obie strony przez 4. Krok 3: x=9. Krok 4: sprawdzenie: 4(9)+4=40, więc równanie jest spełnione.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Reasoning about Solving Równania (Part 1). Nie wykonuj działania tylko po jednej stronie równania bez uzasadnienia. Redukuj wyłącznie wyrazy podobne. Przy mnożeniu nawiasu przez liczbę ujemną pomnóż każdy składnik w nawiasie.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Reasoning about Solving Równania (Part 1). Rozpoznaj strukturę algebraiczną, konsekwentnie zastosuj własności lub działania odwrotne, rozwiąż albo uprość i sprawdź wynik przez podstawienie lub inne równoważne sprawdzenie.

translations.title: Reasoning about Solving Equations (Part 2)
translations.explanation: Reasoning about Solving Equations (Part 2) is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Expressions, Equations, and Inequalities”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.EE.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities. a. Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach. For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width? b. Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Reasoning about Solving Equations (Part 2). An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 2x + 3 = 9. Subtract 3 and divide by 2; the solution is x = 3. Example 2: Solve 6x + 8 = 44. Subtract 8 and divide by 6; the solution is x = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 3 from both sides to get 2x = 6. Step 2: divide both sides by 2. Step 3: x=3. Step 4: substitute: 2(3)+3=9, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 8 from both sides to get 6x = 36. Step 2: divide both sides by 6. Step 3: x=6. Step 4: substitute: 6(6)+8=44, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Reasoning about Solving Equations (Part 2). Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Reasoning about Solving Equations (Part 2). Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation. translations.title: Finding Solutions to Inequalities in Context
translations.explanation: Finding Solutions to Inequalities in Context is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Expressions, Equations, and Inequalities”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.EE.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities. a. Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach. For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width? b. Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Finding Solutions to Inequalities in Context. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 2x + 6 = 22. Subtract 6 and divide by 2; the solution is x = 8. Example 2: Solve 6x + 6 = 60. Subtract 6 and divide by 6; the solution is x = 9.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 6 from both sides to get 2x = 16. Step 2: divide both sides by 2. Step 3: x=8. Step 4: substitute: 2(8)+6=22, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 6 from both sides to get 6x = 54. Step 2: divide both sides by 6. Step 3: x=9. Step 4: substitute: 6(9)+6=60, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Finding Solutions to Inequalities in Context. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Finding Solutions to Inequalities in Context. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

translations.title: Subtraction in Equivalent Expressions
translations.explanation: Subtraction in Equivalent Expressions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Expressions, Equations, and Inequalities”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.EE.A.1, CCSS:7.NS.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients. Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram. a. Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0. For example, a hydrogen atom has 0 charge because its two constituents are oppositely charged. b. Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts. c. Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p – q = p + (–q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts. d. Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Subtraction in Equivalent Expressions. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 5x + 6 = 41. Subtract 6 and divide by 5; the solution is x = 7. Example 2: Solve 3x + 8 = 29. Subtract 8 and divide by 3; the solution is x = 7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 6 from both sides to get 5x = 35. Step 2: divide both sides by 5. Step 3: x=7. Step 4: substitute: 5(7)+6=41, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 8 from both sides to get 3x = 21. Step 2: divide both sides by 3. Step 3: x=7. Step 4: substitute: 3(7)+8=29, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Subtraction in Equivalent Expressions. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.

translations.title: Adjacent Angles
translations.explanation: Adjacent Angles is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Angles, Triangles, and Prisms”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.G.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Adjacent Angles. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 6 and 7 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 6 × 7 = 42 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 5 and 5 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 5 × 5 = 25 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 6 and 7. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 42. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 5 and 5. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 25. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Adjacent Angles. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Adjacent Angles. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

Krok 4: zauważ, że obrót figury nie zmienia jej własności. Krok 1: rozpoznaj cechy definiujące: cztery boki i cztery kąty proste. Krok 2: użyj długości 5 i 5. Krok 3: pomnóż i otrzymaj pole 25. translations.title: Using Equations to Solve for Unknown Angles
translations.explanation: Using Equations to Solve for Unknown Angles is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Angles, Triangles, and Prisms”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.EE.B.4, CCSS:7.G.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities. a. Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach. For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width? b. Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions. Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Using Equations to Solve for Unknown Angles. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 6x + 4 = 46. Subtract 4 and divide by 6; the solution is x = 7. Example 2: Solve 6x + 1 = 37. Subtract 1 and divide by 6; the solution is x = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 4 from both sides to get 6x = 42. Step 2: divide both sides by 6. Step 3: x=7. Step 4: substitute: 6(7)+4=46, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 1 from both sides to get 6x = 36. Step 2: divide both sides by 6. Step 3: x=6. Step 4: substitute: 6(6)+1=37, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Using Equations to Solve for Unknown Angles. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Using Equations to Solve for Unknown Angles. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

translations.title: Building Polygons (Part 1)
translations.explanation: Building Polygons (Part 1) is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Angles, Triangles, and Prisms”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.G.A.2, CCSS:7.NS.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Draw (freehand, with ruler and protractor, and with technology) geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle. Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram. a. Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0. For example, a hydrogen atom has 0 charge because its two constituents are oppositely charged. b. Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts. c. Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p – q = p + (–q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts. d. Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Building Polygons (Part 1). Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 9 and 4 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 9 × 4 = 36 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 3 and 3 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 3 × 3 = 9 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 9 and 4. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 36. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 3 and 3. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 9. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Building Polygons (Part 1). Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Building Polygons (Part 1). Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń formułuje pytania statystyczne, opisuje rozkłady, porównuje dane i wykorzystuje modele losowe, uwzględniając zmienność zamiast pojedynczych wartości. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Statystyka i prawdopodobieństwo — What Are Probabilities?. Dane opisuj w kontekście, uwzględniając miary środka, rozproszenie, kształt rozkładu i wartości nietypowe. Prawdopodobieństwo mieści się między 0 a 1. Krok 4: odejmij minimum 9 od maksimum 15 i otrzymaj rozstęp 6. Krok 1: sprawdź, że jest 5 obserwacji. Krok 2: suma wynosi 51. Krok 3: podziel przez 5 i otrzymaj średnią 10.2. translations.title: Estimating Probabilities Through Repeated Experiments
translations.explanation: Estimating Probabilities Through Repeated Experiments is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Probability and Sampling”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.SP.C.5, CCSS:7.SP.C.6, CCSS:7.SP.C.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event. Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability. For example, when rolling a number cube 600 times, predict that a 3 or 6 would be rolled roughly 200 times, but probably not exactly 200 times. Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy. a. Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events. For example, if a student is selected at random from a class, find the probability that Jane will be selected and the probability that a girl will be selected. b. Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process. For example, find the approximate probab... Instructional focus: Students formulate statistical questions, summarize distributions, compare data, and use chance models to reason from variability rather than from isolated values. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Estimating Probabilities Through Repeated Experiments. Describe data with context, center, spread, shape, and unusual values as appropriate. Probability is between 0 and 1. Experimental results vary, so conclusions should distinguish observed data from what a model predicts.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For the data [11, 13, 15, 15, 17], the mean is (11 + 13 + 15 + 15 + 17)/5 = 14.2. The range is 17 - 11 = 6. Example 2: For the data [4, 6, 8, 8, 10], the mean is (4 + 6 + 8 + 8 + 10)/5 = 7.2. The range is 10 - 4 = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 71. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 14.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 11 from maximum 17 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context. Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 36. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 7.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 4 from maximum 10 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Estimating Probabilities Through Repeated Experiments. Do not report a statistic without saying what it represents. Do not assume a small sample must match the theoretical probability exactly. Check whether comparisons use the same scale and whether the sample supports the conclusion.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Estimating Probabilities Through Repeated Experiments. Connect the question to an appropriate representation or statistic, calculate carefully, describe variability, and make a conclusion that stays within the evidence.

translations.title: Simulating Multi-step Experiments
translations.explanation: Simulating Multi-step Experiments is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Probability and Sampling”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.SP.C.8. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation. a. Understand that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs. b. Represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams. For an event described in everyday language (e.g., “rolling double sixes”), identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event. c. Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events. For example, use random digits as a simulation tool to approximate the answer to the question: If 40% of donors have type A blood, what is the probability that it will take at least 4 donors to find one with type A blood? Instructional focus: Students formulate statistical questions, summarize distributions, compare data, and use chance models to reason from variability rather than from isolated values. translations.title: Planning Recipes
translations.explanation: Planning Recipes is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting it All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.RP.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems. Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error. Instructional focus: Students compare quantities multiplicatively and use equivalent ratios, unit rates, tables, graphs, equations, and percentages to describe proportional relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Planning Recipes. A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios scale both quantities by the same nonzero factor. In y = kx, k is the constant of proportionality and equals the unit rate when the variables have the corresponding units.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The ratio 7:10 is equivalent to 14:20 because both terms were multiplied by 2. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 10/7 = 1.43. Example 2: The ratio 7:8 is equivalent to 28:32 because both terms were multiplied by 4. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 8/7 = 1.14.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: preserve the order 7:10. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 2. Step 3: obtain 14:20. Step 4: divide 10 by 7 to obtain unit rate 1.43 and retain the contextual units. Step 1: preserve the order 7:8. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 4. Step 3: obtain 28:32. Step 4: divide 8 by 7 to obtain unit rate 1.14 and retain the contextual units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Planning Recipes. Do not compare ratios using only one component. Keep units and order consistent. A relationship with a nonzero intercept is not directly proportional, even if some pairs look almost proportional.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Planning Recipes. State the ratio with units and order, find an equivalent ratio or unit rate, represent the relationship, and check that both quantities scale consistently.

translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 7:10. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 2. Krok 3: otrzymaj 14:20. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Fermi Problems. Position on the number line determines order. Opposites are the same distance from zero on different sides. Absolute value is distance from zero. Operation rules must be connected to direction, magnitude, or properties rather than memorized without meaning.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Start at -3 on the number line and add 9. Moving 9 units to the right lands at 6, so -3 + 9 = 6. The absolute value |-3| = 3. Example 2: Start at -11 on the number line and add 3. Moving 3 units to the right lands at -8, so -11 + 3 = -8. The absolute value |-11| = 11.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: locate -3. Step 2: addition of positive 9 means move right 9 units. Step 3: arrive at 6. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-3|=3 records distance from zero, not the sign. Step 1: locate -11. Step 2: addition of positive 3 means move right 3 units. Step 3: arrive at -8. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-11|=11 records distance from zero, not the sign.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Fermi Problems. Do not confuse a negative sign with an instruction to subtract. When comparing negative numbers, the number farther left is smaller. Keep exact values, such as radicals, when a decimal approximation is not required.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Fermi Problems. Represent the numbers on an appropriate scale, apply operation and order rules carefully, and check sign and magnitude before accepting the result.

translations.title: More Expressions and Equations
translations.explanation: More Expressions and Equations is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting it All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.EE.A.1, CCSS:7.EE.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients. Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities. a. Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach. For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width? b. Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: More Expressions and Equations. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 6x + 6 = 18. Subtract 6 and divide by 6; the solution is x = 2. Example 2: Solve 3x + 8 = 35. Subtract 8 and divide by 3; the solution is x = 9.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 6 from both sides to get 6x = 12. Step 2: divide both sides by 6. Step 3: x=2. Step 4: substitute: 6(2)+6=18, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 8 from both sides to get 3x = 27. Step 2: divide both sides by 3. Step 3: x=9. Step 4: substitute: 3(9)+8=35, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: More Expressions and Equations. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: More Expressions and Equations. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

translations.title: Measurement Error (Part 1)
translations.explanation: Measurement Error (Part 1) is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting it All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:7.RP.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems. Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Measurement Error (Part 1). A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios scale both quantities by the same nonzero factor. In y = kx, k is the constant of proportionality and equals the unit rate when the variables have the corresponding units.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The ratio 7:5 is equivalent to 14:10 because both terms were multiplied by 2. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 5/7 = 0.714. Example 2: The ratio 6:6 is equivalent to 12:12 because both terms were multiplied by 2. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 6/6 = 1.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: preserve the order 7:5. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 2. Step 3: obtain 14:10. Step 4: divide 5 by 7 to obtain unit rate 0.714 and retain the contextual units. Step 1: preserve the order 6:6. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 2. Step 3: obtain 12:12. Step 4: divide 6 by 6 to obtain unit rate 1 and retain the contextual units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Measurement Error (Part 1). Do not compare ratios using only one component. Keep units and order consistent. A relationship with a nonzero intercept is not directly proportional, even if some pairs look almost proportional.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Measurement Error (Part 1). State the ratio with units and order, find an equivalent ratio or unit rate, represent the relationship, and check that both quantities scale consistently.
